books.section: Topic 6.11 Reform in the Gilded Age
The Rise of the Modern American City

primary_sources: Jane Addams, Twenty Years at Hull-House (1910)

stimulus.text:
“At a meeting of working girls held at Hull-House during a strike in a large shoe factory, the discussions made it clear that the strikers who had been most easily frightened, and therefore first to capitulate, were naturally those girls who were paying board and were afraid of being put out if they fell too far behind. After a recital of a case of peculiar hardship one of them exclaimed: “Wouldn’t it be fine if we had a boarding club of our own, and then we could stand by each other in a time like this?” After that events moved quickly. We read aloud together Beatrice Potter’s little book on “Coöperation,” and discussed all the difficulties and fascinations of such an undertaking, and on the first of May, 1891, two comfortable apartments near Hull-House were rented and furnished. The Settlement was responsible for the furniture and paid the first month’s rent, but beyond that the members managed the club themselves.”

(Jane Addams, Twenty Years at Hull-House, 1910, Chapter VII)
stimulus.source_note: Jane Addams, Twenty Years at Hull-House (1910), Chapter VII, “Some Early Undertakings at Hull-House,” p. 136. Public domain; wording checked against the University of Pennsylvania digital text. The book was published in 1910 and recalls the boarding club founded May 1, 1891.

stem: The boarding club described in the passage best shows that settlement workers aimed to do which of the following?

options.text: Pay striking workers so they could hold out longer
options.misconception: The Settlement paid for furniture and the first month’s rent, not the strikers’ wages.

options.text: Replace the shoe factory with a worker-owned business
options.misconception: The club was a boarding house for workers, not a new factory.

options.text: Help workers support one another through their own cooperative effort
Move striking workers out of Chicago to safer towns
options.misconception: The two apartments were near Hull-House, keeping workers in the neighborhood.

rationales.A: The Settlement paid for furniture and one month’s rent. It did not pay the strikers’ wages.
rationales.B: The club gave workers a place to live together. It did not take over the shoe factory.
rationales.C: The girls asked for a club of their own so they could stand by each other, and the members ran it themselves.
rationales.D: The two apartments were near Hull-House. The club kept workers in the neighborhood, not away from it.
rationales.general:
Start with what the girls themselves asked for.
1. The frightened strikers were girls paying board, afraid of losing their rooms.
2. One girl proposed a boarding club of their own so they could stand by each other.
3. The Settlement furnished the rooms and paid the first month’s rent, then stepped back.
4. The members managed the club themselves, so the help was cooperation, not charity handed down.
Remember: settlement work meant living beside workers and backing their own efforts.
